en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Effects of Good and Evil Spoken by the Buddha.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immense assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas as he preached the Dharma.
Listen with single-minded attention.
At that time, Ānanda, for the sake of sentient beings, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Now we see that those born equally as humans within this world are some handsome and some ugly; some strong and some weak; some poor and some wealthy; some suffering and some happy; some noble and some lowly. Their voices differ and their languages vary. Some live for a hundred years without dying, while others perish early at thirty, or die prematurely at fifteen, or even fall from the womb.

"There are those who are upright and virtuous yet poor and lowly; those who are ugly and deformed yet wealthy and noble. There are those who are powerful and strong yet base and inferior; those who are weak and frail yet occupy high positions. There are those who suffer yet live long lives; those who enjoy pleasure yet die young. There are those who practice goodness yet meet with misfortune; those who commit evil yet receive blessings and profit. There are those who are fat, with white eyes and squinting stares; those who are dark and thin yet charming and graceful. There are those who, though short and small, are full of spirit and vigor; and those who, though tall and large, serve as others' slaves."

"There are those with abundant sons and daughters, and there are those who are solitary and alone; there are those wandering abroad, emaciated by hunger and cold, and there are those within the palace or at court, enjoying food and clothing to their heart's content; there are those who were poor and lowly in youth but become wealthy and noble in old age, and there are those who, though innocent and without fault, suffer unjust imprisonment; there are those where father and son are kind and filial, discussing the scriptures and explaining their meanings, and there are those where brothers are estranged, falling into mutual strife and contention; there are those who dwell securely in established homes with all manner of abundance, and there are those who have no houses of their own, drifting and lodging wherever they may be."

"There are those who dwell with crows, nest with deer, and associate with beasts of prey; there are those who wear fur and consume blood, being ignorant of written characters. There are those who sit upright and receive their retribution, and those who work as laborers with no land of their own. There are those who are intelligent and lofty-minded, and those who are dull-witted and lacking wisdom. There are those who obtain results only through diligent effort, and those for whom things arrive spontaneously without seeking. There are those who are wealthy yet stingy and greedy, and those who are poor yet fond of giving. There are those whose speech is harmonious and conciliatory, and those whose words are like thorns. There are those who are loved and respected by others, and those whom the multitude avoids from afar. There are those who nourish their lives with a compassionate heart, and those who kill living beings without restraint. There are those who are broad-minded and gather a following, and those who are abandoned by all."

"There are those where mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law hate one another, and those where sisters-in-law frolic together; there are those who delight in hearing the Dharma, and those who fall asleep upon hearing the sutras; there are those who are ill-mannered warriors, and those who are fond of studying the meaning of the texts; there are those who take on the forms of beasts and various other species."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and effects in detail; if the great assembly hears this, they will single-mindedly follow what is wholesome.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“As for the different ways in which retributions are received, as you have asked, these all arise because the application of the mind in previous lives was not equal; it is for this reason that what is received differs in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations.”

Those who are upright and handsome in this life come from practicing patience; those who are ugly come from harboring anger; those who are poor come from stinginess and greed; those who are noble and high-born come from performing prostrations; those who are lowly and base come from arrogance; those who are tall and large come from showing respect; those who are short of stature come from disparaging the Dharma; those who are fierce and cruel come from being sheep; and those who are dark-skinned and deformed come from obstructing the light of the Buddha.

"To have tight lips comes from having tasted food offered in a communal assembly; to have red eyes comes from begrudging the light of fire; to have night-blindness like a sparrow comes from sewing together the eyes of hawks; to be mute comes from slandering the Dharma; to be deaf comes from taking no pleasure in hearing the Dharma; to have missing teeth comes from delighting in biting bone and flesh; to have a blocked nose comes from burning unpleasant incense as an offering to the Buddha; to have cleft lips comes from piercing the gills of fish; to have yellow hair comes from hog-tethering pigs; to have pierced ears comes from boring holes in one's own ears."

"To become a snake is due to having worn light clothing while rushing past a Buddha image; to become black-skinned is due to having entered a house where a Buddha image was placed beneath the eaves and been smoked out; to become a hunchback or a cripple is due to failing to rise when seeing one's teacher; to become a person with a crooked back is due to entering or exiting wearing light clothing while turning one's back on a Buddha image; to become a person with a deformed shin or forehead is due to failing to prostrate before a Buddha upon seeing Him and instead grasping His hand to strike one's own forehead; to become a person with a short neck is due to shrinking one's head and fleeing when seeing a venerable elder; to become a person with heart disease is due to hacking or stabbing the bodies of sentient beings; to become a person with leprosy is due to taking the property of others unjustly; to become a person with coughing fits is due to giving cold food to others during the winter months."
“Those who become men without sons or daughters come from killing the offspring of other birds;
those who have many children come from delighting in nurturing living beings; those who have long lives come from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
those who have short lives come from taking life; and those who become very wealthy come from practicing giving (*dāna*).”
Those who come from among the donors are those who, as humans, gave horses and carriages to the Triple Gem;
those who are intelligent and wise come from among those who studied and recited the sutras; those who are dull-witted and obtuse come from among the animals;
those who are slaves come from among those burdened by debt; and those who are restless and frantic come from among the monkeys.
Those who suffer from leprosy come from having caused the destruction of the Triple Gem;
those whose hands and feet are impaired come from binding and restraining the hands and feet of sentient beings; those who are of an evil temperament come from being like snakes and scorpions;
those who possess all six sense faculties come from upholding the precepts; and those whose faculties are incomplete [come from violating them].
Those with deformed feet come from those who broke the precepts.

Those who are unclean come from pigs. Those who delight in singing and dancing come from performers. Those who are excessively greedy come from dogs. Those who have goiters on their necks come from those who ate alone. Those whose breath is foul-smelling come from those who used abusive language. Those whose male organs are incomplete come from those who castrated pigs and dogs.

Those who have short tongues in this life come from having stolen and slandered their elders in private places. Those who take pleasure in committing adultery with the wives of others die and fall among geese and ducks;

those who take pleasure in committing incest with members of their own ninefold kin die and fall among sparrows. Those who are stingy with scriptures and conceal their wisdom, refusing to teach it to others, die and become insects within earthenware or wood. Those who delight in carrying bows and arrows or riding mounts die and fall among the six barbarian tribes. Those who delight in hunting and killing living beings die and fall among jackals and wolves. Those who delight in wearing flowers grown on wounds die and become *zhaiseng* insects. Those who delight in wearing long robes die and become long-tailed insects.
"One who delights in eating while lying down falls into the womb of a pig after death; one who is fond of wearing dyed garments becomes a speckled bird after death;
one who delights in mimicking the speech of others to mock them becomes a parrot after death;
one who delights in slandering others falls into the midst of the virulent poison of a python after death; and one who causes needless distress to others becomes a vexing insect after death."
Those who delight in spreading malicious rumors die and become owls; those who delight in speaking words that bring calamity and misfortune to others die and become wild foxes;
those who delight in terrifying people die and become *chiao-lu* insects;

those who wore wooden clogs when entering a temple in their previous lives are reborn in this life among horses with split hooves; and those who delighted in passing gas during the previous month [are reborn as such].

Those who have now become *kṣudraka* insects were, in their previous lives, those who used the mortars and millstones belonging to the Saṃgha; those who have now become *mūrdha-ghāta* insects were, in their previous lives, those who measured out people's food;
and those who have now become woodpeckers were, in their previous lives, those who [appropriated] others' food.
"Those who misappropriated the Sangha's water have now become fish and turtles in the water; those who defiled the Sangha's grounds have become insects in the cesspool;
those who stole the Sangha's fruit and cakes have become insects that eat soil; those who pilfered the Sangha's property have now become oxen, donkeys, and millstones;
those who forcibly begged loans from the Sangha have now become white doves; and those who reviled and insulted the assembly..."
Those who were monks have now become worms in the nape of an ox; those who ate the vegetables of the Sangha have become worms in sweet flag;
those who sat upon the beds of the Sangha have become earthworms; those who used the miscellaneous belongings of the Sangha have become moths that cast themselves into fire;
and those who entered the temple with their bones cracked and smeared with hūpíng powder and vermilion lips have now become long-beaked birds.
Those who enter a temple today are depicted as red *mǎo* birds wearing multicolored robes;
those who stay overnight in a temple with their spouses are depicted as blue-headed *tái* insects;
those who sit with their backs turned toward a Buddha stupa are depicted as camel-bodied creatures; and those who enter a pagoda or monastery wearing shoes and boots are depicted as shrimp.
The *mā* insect, which spoke disruptively while listening to the Dharma, has now become a hundred-tongued bird;
those who defiled nuns of pure conduct die and fall into the Iron Cave Hell, where a million sword-wheels descend all at once to hack their bodies to pieces.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"According to what the Buddha has taught, the offense of misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha is indeed extremely grave.
If this is the case, how can the four classes of donors go to the monastery to pay their respects and offer prostrations?"
The Buddha said:
"When going to a monastic community (saṃghārāma), there are two kinds of mind:
first, the wholesome mind; [second, the unwholesome mind]."
The second is the evil mind. What is called the wholesome mind?

It is when, having entered the midst of the Saṃgha, one sees the Buddha and prostrates; sees the Saṃgha and shows them respect; requests scriptures, inquires about their meaning, receives the precepts, and performs repentance; gives away wealth and property to support the Three Jewels; and protects and upholds the Great Dharma without begrudging one's own body or life.

For such a person, with every step they take, paradise comes of its own accord; in the future, they will receive the fruit [of their merit] just like Jyotiṣka. Such a person is called the most supreme virtuous one.
What is meant by an "evil mind"?

It refers to when sentient beings enter a monastery and do nothing but beg and borrow from the assembly of monks; or seek out the faults of the monks with the sole intent to destroy them; or consume the food of the Sangha without any sense of shame, carrying away cakes, fruits, and vegetables to their homes.

Such a person, upon death, falls into the Iron Ball Hell, where they undergo every torment—boiling cauldrons, glowing embers, mountains of knives, and forests of swords; such a one is called the most base and evil of men.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“I exhort those who will be my disciples in future ages: be cautious and do not offend the Three Jewels; strive with diligence to achieve perfection and do not give rise to a regressive mind.
Those who act according to the Buddha’s words will undoubtedly attain deliverance when Maitreya appears in the world.”
The Buddha said:
"One who strips others of their clothing in this life will, after death, fall into the Cold Ice Hell and further be reborn as a silkworm to be boiled and stripped by others;
one who does not rejoice in lighting lamps to illuminate the scriptures and images in this life will, after death, fall into the Dark Hell between the Iron Ring Mountains."
Those who in this life slaughter, butcher, or maim sentient beings will, upon death, fall into the hell of the Mountain of Knives and the Forest of Swords;
those who in this life delight in hunting with hawks and dogs or shooting arrows will, upon death, fall into the hell of the Iron Saw;
and those who in this life engage extensively in perverse conduct will, upon death, fall into the hell of the Copper Pillar and the Iron Bed.
Those who keep many wives in this life will, after death, fall into the Iron Mill Hell;
those who keep many husbands in this life will, after death, fall into the Venomous Snake Hell;
and those who burn eggs in this life will, after death, fall into the Ash River Hell.
"Those who today castrate pigs or chickens will, upon death, fall into the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons;
those who today castrate pigs or dogs will, upon death, fall into the Hell of Sharp Stones;
those who today drink alcohol and become intoxicated and deranged will, upon death, fall into the Hell of Drinking Molten Copper."
Those who in this life cut or maim living beings will, after death, fall into the Iron Wheel Hell;
those who in this life steal fruit or confections belonging to the Sangha will, after death, fall into the Iron Ball Hell;
and those who in this life eat the entrails or meat of pigs or dogs will, after death, fall into the Excrement and Urine Hell.
If in this present life one eats raw fish, upon death one will fall into the Hell of the Forest of Knives and Sword-Trees.
If in this present life one acts as a stepmother who flatters and harms the children of the biological mother, upon death one will fall into the Hell of the Fiery Chariot.
If in this present life one engages in double-tongued speech to incite strife and discord, upon death one will fall into the Hell of the Iron Plow.
Those who revile others with both body and mouth in this life will, after death, fall into the Hell of the Plucked Tongue;
those who engage in much false speech in this life will, after death, fall into the Hell of Iron Needles;
and those who kill living beings to sacrifice to heterodox deities in this life will, after death, fall into the Hell of the Iron Mortar.
"In this life, those who act as female shamans (*shimo*) and deceive others with ghostly speech to take their property fall, upon death, into the Flesh Mountain Hell (*Nishizai Jigoku*).

In this life, those who act as female shamans and deceive others by feigning sleep with eyes closed while claiming to ascend to heaven to fetch the souls of the deceased fall, upon death, into the Severed Waist Hell (*Chōkō Jigoku*)."

In this present life, one may act as a "master mother" (shimu), teaching others to kill living beings to seek great divine powers, whether for the Five Paths, local deities, village spirits, or the male and female spirits of the *āpasmāra* class; all such practices are merely delusions used to deceive simpletons. Upon death, they fall into the *Khara* Hell, where various hell-wardens hack and chop their bodies, and iron-beaked birds peck out both their eyes.

Those who in this life act as shamans, or bury the dead, or practice geomancy for the auspiciousness or misfortune of dwellings, or calculate the advantages of the five surnames, or perform rites to settle dragons and thank the silkworm deities, or suppress calamities and misfortunes—deceiving the ignorant to take their wealth and falsely uttering words of good and bad fortune—such persons, upon death, shall fall into the Iron and Copper Hells. There, immeasurable evil birds will gather upon their bodies to devour their flesh; they will peck away their bones and sinews until suffering becomes endless.

If, in this present life, one acts as a physician yet fails to cure illnesses and instead deceives others to take their property, upon death they will fall into the Needle-and-Moxibustion Hell, where their entire body burns with fire.

If, in this present life, one destroys stupas or ruins temples, acts rebelliously toward teachers and monks, or is unfilial toward one’s parents, upon death they will fall into the Avīci Great Earth Hell. There they will fully experience the eight great hells and further enter all the minor hells—entering all one hundred and thirty-six locations—and remain there for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to five kalpas. Only after that may they emerge; if they encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they may resolve to attain Bodhicitta, but if they do not meet such a person, they will fall back into hell.
The Buddha said:
"Those who, having become human, have bodies that are foul-smelling and filthy, and who are prone to anger and difficult to reconcile, come from among camels.
Those who, having become human, delight in reckless conduct and voracious eating, and do not avoid perilous difficulties, come from among horses."
Those who are capable of enduring cold and heat but lack a mind of mindfulness have come from among oxen.
Those who speak loudly without shame, harbor many attachments, and fail to distinguish between right and wrong have come from among donkeys.
Those who are constantly greedy for meat and act without fear come from among lions.
Those who are tall-bodied with round eyes, frequent the wilderness, and harbor hatred and jealousy toward their wives and children come from among tigers.
Those who have long body hair and small eyes, and who do not delight in staying in one place, come from among the flying birds.
Those whose nature is ungrateful and who take pleasure in killing harmful insects, come from among the wild foxes.
Those who are brave and robust, have little lustful desire, and do not love their wives or children, come from among wolves.
Those who do not take pleasure in fine clothing, who lie in wait to catch those who commit illicit acts, and who were fierce-eyed and prone to anger in childhood, come from among dogs.
Those who are fond of lustful desires and delight in discussing what others love have come from among the parrots.
Those who are fond of people and whose speech in assemblies is often tedious have come from among the owls.
"If one is small in stature, has a lustful disposition, and becomes mentally deluded upon seeing forms without concentration, they have come from among sparrows.
If one has red eyes and short teeth, spits when speaking, and wraps their body around themselves while lying down, they have come from among snakes and vipers."
When speaking with others, one becomes angry and fails to examine the meaning of what is said; such a person who emits fiery venom from their mouth comes from among scorpions.
When dwelling alone, one is greedy for food and sleeps little at night; such a person comes from among wildcats.
"One who breaks through walls for others to commit theft, covets wealth, and harbors malice toward all without distinction between kin and stranger, comes from among the rats.
The Buddha said:

"One who destroys stupas or monasteries, or conceals the property of the Triple Gem to use for oneself, will fall into the Avīci Great Hell after death. Upon emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal—namely, a pigeon, a sparrow, a mandarin duck, a ruddy sheldrake, a parrot, a blue jay, a fish, a turtle, a monkey, a deer, or a roe deer."
If one obtains a human body, one may take the form of a eunuch, a woman with two sexual organs, one without organs, or a prostitute.
Those who are prone to anger will, upon death, fall among the venomous snakes, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, wildcats, hawks, and roosters;
or, if they obtain a human body, they will be those who delight in raising chickens and pigs, or become butchers, hunters, fishermen, or prison guards.

Those who are foolish and do not understand the principles of reality will, upon death, fall into the forms of elephants, pigs, oxen, sheep, water buffaloes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and the like;
even if they obtain a human body, they will be deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or afflicted with back sores, their faculties incomplete, and thus unable to receive the Dharma.
Those who are arrogant and conceited will, upon death, fall among the dung-worms, camels, donkeys, dogs, and horses;
if they are born among humans, they will take the form of slaves or beggars, impoverished and despised by all.

Those who, for the sake of official position or influence, greedily seize the property of the people, die and fall into the Flesh-Mountain Hell, where hundreds of thousands of people cut off their flesh to eat.
Those who in this life take pleasure in establishing others [in positions of power] die and fall among white elephants, lying with their legs straight and unable to turn their heads.

Those who break the precepts by eating at night in this present life will, after death, fall among the hungry ghosts; for millions upon millions of years they shall not obtain food or drink, and when they move about, flames will issue from their heads.
Those who, in this present life, take pleasure in sitting with their bodies exposed will, after death, become cold owls.

Those who, in this present life, carry away the leftovers of offerings and food will, after death, fall into the Heat Iron Hell; furthermore, if they are reborn among humans, they will suffer from throat-obstruction diseases and die prematurely.

If one bows to the Buddha with this present body but the head does not touch the ground, at death one will fall into the Inverted Hanging Hell; furthermore, if reborn among humans, one will frequently be subject to deception.
If one bows to the Buddha with this present body but does not join the palms, at death one will fall into a frontier land, where although much labor and effort are expended, nothing is harvested.

If one does not rise when hearing the sound of the bell in this present life, after death they will fall among the pythons; their bodies will become so vast that they are devoured by myriad small insects.

If one stands with hands clasped in reverence to the Buddha in this present life, after death they will fall into the Hell of Reverse Bondage, and even if reborn among humans, they will meet with calamitous misfortunes.
"One who now joins their palms and prostrates with the five limbs to the Buddha with a sincere heart will always abide in nobility and constantly experience happiness.
One who is currently fierce in anger and gluttonous for food has come from a state of madness."
If one’s eyes are squinting and distorted in this life, it results from having looked askance at the wives and daughters of others out of depravity.
If one protects one’s own wife while reviling one’s parents in this life, upon death one will fall into the Hell of Severed Tongues.

If one's current body is like water placed within wine and sold to others, after death one will become an insect in water; furthermore, one may be reborn among humans with dropsy and die from the failure of breath.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The various sufferings just described all arise from the karma of the ten unwholesome actions; the superior [retribution] is the causal condition for hell, the middling is the causal condition for animals, and the inferior is the causal condition for hungry ghosts.”
Among these, the transgression of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, a short lifespan; [and second, much illness].
Second, they suffer from many illnesses.
The crime of robbery and theft likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits: [the first is] being frequently ill.
First, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
The transgression of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If one is born among humans, one will receive two kinds of retribution:
first, one's wife will not be chaste and virtuous;
second, one will have two wives who quarrel with each other and do not follow one's own wishes.
The sin of lying also causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are frequently subjected to slander.
Second, one is constantly deceived by many people.
The transgression of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
First, one will have a divided retinue;
second, one will have a base and evil retinue.
Furthermore, the sin of harsh speech causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If one is born among humans, two kinds of retributive fruits will be obtained:
first, one will constantly hear unpleasant sounds;
second, all of one’s speech will be perpetually subject to dispute and litigation.
The sin of frivolous speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, there are two kinds of retribution:
first, speaking of what righteous people do not speak of; and second, accepting what they do not say.
Second, all verbal expressions cannot fully describe the offenses of greed and desire;
they likewise cause sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits:
First, they are insatiable in their craving for wealth;
second, they constantly seek much, yet never find what they desire.
The transgression of anger likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If one is born among humans, two kinds of retributive fruits are obtained:
first, one constantly seeks out the faults and shortcomings of others;
second, one is constantly troubled and harmed by others.
The sin of wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are always born into families that hold wrong views.
Second, their minds are constantly crooked and deceitful.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
These ten paths of unwholesome action are all causes and conditions for the great accumulation of suffering."

At that time, among the great assembly, there were those who had committed the ten unwholesome deeds; hearing the Buddha speak of these retributions of suffering in hell, they all wailed loudly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What wholesome deeds must my disciple perform to escape this suffering?
The Buddha said,
"He should further teach and transform all sentient beings so that they may collectively engage in meritorious karma."
How does one cultivate merit?

If there are sentient beings who, in their present life, act as great patrons of transformation and construct stupas and monasteries, they will surely become kings in the future, ruling over the myriad people so that none fail to submit.

Those who in this present life serve as city governors, impartial judges, stewards, or wheel-turning lords will, in future ages, certainly become kings’ ministers, high officials, or magistrates of provinces and districts, possessing robes and horses in abundance and enjoying all their needs to their heart’s content.

Those who, in this present life, lead others by example to perform various meritorious deeds will, in future lives, certainly become wealthy and noble elders; they will be revered by all people, their fourfold paths will be open and unobstructed, and wherever they turn, they will find favorable circumstances.
Those who, in this present life, delight in lighting lamps to continue the light will be born among the devas of the sun and moon, where their own radiance illuminates them.
Those who, in this present life, delight in practicing generosity and sustaining their lives with a compassionate heart will be born into great wealth, where food and clothing come to them naturally.

Now, for one who is fond of giving food and drink to others in this life, celestial cuisine arrives spontaneously wherever they are born; they possess full physical vigor and intelligence, as well as eloquence, and their lifespan is long and far-reaching.
"If one gives to an animal, one receives a hundredfold reward.
If one gives to an icchantika, one receives a thousandfold reward.
If one gives to a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, one receives ten-thousandfold reward."

If one makes offerings to Dharma masters so that they may circulate the Mahāyāna and proclaim the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, thereby causing the great assembly to open their mental eyes, they shall obtain immeasurable retribution.
If one gives to Bodhisattvas or to the Buddhas, the retribution received is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of persons to whom giving results in inexhaustible retribution:
first, the Buddhas; [the second, the Bodhisattvas; and the third, those who have set out on the path].
Second, one's parents; third, the sick.
Even a single meal given as an offering yields immeasurable retribution; how much more so when one is able to give constantly—how could its merit ever be exhausted!
"One who bathes the assembly of monks in this present life will have a handsome countenance wherever they are born, shall be naturally clothed, and will be revered by all people.
One who delights in praising and reciting the sutras and the Dharma in this present life will have a refined and wondrous voice wherever they are born, bringing joy to all who hear it."
Those who in this life take joy in upholding the precepts will be born handsome and most excellent among men.

Those who in this life delight in constructing wells for public benefit, making water jars, planting trees by the roadside to provide shade for all people, will always be born as kings of men in their future lives, with food and drink of a hundred flavors arriving immediately upon their thought.

Those who now joyfully transcribe the sutras and Dharma to bestow as gifts upon others for their reading will, in all places where they are born, possess eloquence and great talent; they will comprehend and realize the teachings they study upon hearing them once; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly provide them with protection; and among all people, they will be the most excellent, always serving as leaders.

If one now delights in building bridges and boats to ferry people across, in whatever place they are born, the seven treasures will be fully present; all people will respect and praise them, never failing to look up to them in reverence, and as they come and go, people will assist them by supporting their entry and exit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In accordance with the causes and effects I have taught throughout the various sūtras, I exhort all sentient beings to read, recite, and practice them so that they may attain liberation from suffering and hardship;
yet if anyone hears this sūtra and gives rise to slander, their tongue shall fall out in this very life."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named, and by what means should it be used to inspire others?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This sutra is titled ‘The Cause and Effect of Good and Evil,’ and it is also titled ‘The Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Vow and Practice. You should receive and uphold it in this way.”

When the Buddha preached this sutra, eighty thousand devas and humans among the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One hundred thousand women manifested the transformation of their female bodies and attained male forms. One thousand two hundred wicked people abandoned their poisonous intentions and came to know their past lives. Immeasurable virtuous people attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) and constantly experienced bliss. Immeasurable upright practitioners were born in various pure lands, where they became companions to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The entire great assembly returned home to perform meritorious deeds, joyfully receiving and practicing [the teaching].
The Scripture on the Causes and Effects of Good and Evil Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One, ends.
